#1730. Fridges and pigs and scoring goals

We live in strange times. Sorry to start your day with this shocking revelation, I realise this is a bit of a bolt from the blue, but it’s fact. All across Europe supermarket fridges are being hacked. What a time to be alive. They used to hack, I dunno, mainframes and banks and shit, but now they’re hacking fridges.

Maybe they just got bored taking billions of made-up money from CryptoSloth and BitWomble and needed a challenge. I feel like fridges ought to be the kind of thing you just can’t hack – beyond unplugging it – but what do I know? Anyway, it’s an example of how the inter-connectivity that brings us all together every day is being weaponised and now the sliced meats in your local store are gone off because Neo pwned some large cold cupboards. As if we don’t have enough to deal with.

Such as all the people who hate the way Arsenal play. Let me be very clear, my days of caring what other people think about this football club, or pretty much anything else that’s important to me, are gone. It’s a waste of time. It’s a bit like quote that’s often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, which says ‘Never wrestle with pigs. You both get dirty and the pig likes it.’

I don’t think he actually said that, but I think we can all connect with the meaning. It applies so much to social media, and to many of the ways we’re exposed to punditry and ‘expert’ analysis in football these days. Like one of those shows where you have a couple of ex-pro pigs bleating on about this and that, and then a collection of other little pigs who support all the clubs argue with them and amongst themselves, and it’s just a pigstravaganza of pointless, inane bollocks but it does #numbers on socials so is seen as valuable #content.

I understand why opposition fans go on and on about how much they hate how Arsenal play. It’s because we win a lot of games. That’s the thing that really irks them. That’s just so basic though, you can’t appear to be clever and an aficionado of the game if you just say ‘I don’t like it when they win’, so it’s dressed up as dismissal of style or something else.

And look, here’s where the strange world we live in comes back into focus. You can, and really should, be able to hold more than one thought in your brain – about football or anything else – that holds true. I absolutely love how good we are defensively. LOVE IT. The commitment with which we are determined not to give the opposition anything is truly something to relish. Players laser-focused on their one on ones; putting bodies on the line to block shots and crosses; 11 players moving like a murmuration of birds because they’re so well drilled and organised; off the awareness and discipline; brilliantly timed tackles and headers and clearances; lads sticking up for each other when the opposition get a bit snide, as we saw on Sunday with Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke refusing to allow their captain to be treated that way; it’s all part of a brilliantly defiant defensive attitude that runs right through this team.

Creating that is not easy. As Arsenal fans we have endured defences that were porous and feeble and, at times, very, very stupid. I do not long for a return to those times. Over the years Mikel Arteta has assembled a collection of players who cannot wait to go out there and do the dirty work of defending, and it runs from front to back because that’s what he demands. If it was that easy, everyone would do it, so to castigate a team’s brilliance in one department because you just lost to them without a shot on target just comes across as sour grapes.

Here’s the other thought though. I’d really like us to be a bit better from an attacking perspective, and when I look at this team and what it’s capable of, there’s no question the forward line remains the area where you can see the room for improvement. We defend as well as we do because, more often than you or I might like, we have to – because we live through games of fine margins. A 1-0 to the Arsenal is part of our history, hard-wired into our supporter DNA (particularly if you’re of a particular vintage), but I can’t lie and wish there weren’t a few more 3-0s to the Arsenal.

I’m absolutely certain Mikel Arteta would like that too, and I think it’s a bit too easy to say that this is a team that plays precisely the football he wants it to play. He is, as we all understand, an arch pragmatist, so what we get is a team that leans into its strengths, as laid out above. He is characterised as a defensive coach, which I get, but a few seasons ago we found an attacking cocktail that drove a title challenge, and saw us score more goals that year than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004 (91 to 73).

I think he wants both. He wants that parsimony at the back and the firepower up front. Unfortunately, forward line recruitment is the most difficult part of transfer business, and while he as manager has a part to play in that, as a club our track record is quite poor in that regard. This summer’s window was a complete bust from an attacking perspective, not a good look when you’re pursuing players like Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez. When you then let three forwards go and add just one, there are questions to be asked of the people in charge. Arteta among them, of course, but he’s not the one whose job it is to get the deals done.

It’s why there are so many conversations around January, and what we might do. We see other clubs recruit forwards who produce on a consistent basis, while ours too often struggle to find that end product. Is it our system? Would these players find it hard to get those goals for us? Reasonable questions, but the bottom line in my opinion is that we have A+ options at the back and in midfield, while in that front three we’re a bit C-. That’s where the room for improvement is, that’s where the recruitment needs to be better (certainly better than no recruitment at all), and that’s how the games we currently win by a single goal margin, often by virtue of our defensive strength, become a bit more routine.

Simplistic? Yes. Easier said than done? Quite probably. But necessary? Absolutely. Until then though, expect more defensive masterclasses, more pig wrestling, and perhaps someone could hack our own Swedish fridge into scoring a few more goals. Worth a try!

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. I just have a small favour to ask. Arseblog has been nominated for Best Fan Media (Fran Merida) in the 2026 FSA Awards. We’re trying to retain our title, so if you could take a moment to give us a vote that would be much appreciated. You can do that here – https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/fsa-awards-2026

#1729. Mauricio Pochettino is adored by his players, big on culture and good vibes, not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools - exactly what dysfunctional Man United are crying out for

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 17:59 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 10 November 2026

After one press conference during Mauricio Pochettino’s ill-fated spell at Chelsea, he hosted an Argentinian-style BBQ for approximately 130 people, including his players and their families, under a marquee set up in the first-team car park at their training ground.

Returning to the room and the assembled throng of journalists still working, Pochettino popped a large plate of sausages and steaks down on the desk. He insisted it did not constitute bribery for better coverage of him. Just thought we might like to join.

This was Pochettino personified. Big on togetherness. Insisted on creating a homely environment for everyone. Believed a harmonious culture at Cobham would help performances on the pitch. Even kept a big box of lemons in his office because he reckoned they harnessed ‘energia universal’. He emphasised the importance of a good mood.

Goodness knows that’s what Manchester United need right now. And if they do decide to dismiss Michael Carrick, the prospect of managing possibly the biggest club in world football would not faze Pochettino – now the bookies’ favourite to take over.

Indeed, the 54-year-old would relish the challenge.

A few days before USA’s World Cup victory against Bosnia and Herzegovina to reach the last 16 at this summer’s tournament, coach Pochettino invited a small group of journalists to interview him at the team hotel – the Ritz-Carlton in Laguna Niguel, overlooking the Pacific Ocean 50 miles south of Los Angeles.

Manchester United could do with a dose of Mauricio Pochettino - and he would relish the challenge

The United States manager - who would cost around £7.5million to release - has openly admitted he wants to lead them in the future

Towards the end of the interview the Manchester United job came up in conversation. Pochettino turned to his long-time assistant coach Jesus Perez and said: ‘One day, your dream comes true... you go to Manchester United!’.

The Argentine clarified somewhat by explaining that Perez, while living in London, would often visit Manchester on days off to visit the National Football Museum. Perez responded with a smile: ‘United should have got you’.

One thing about Pochettino that Manchester United players will soon figure out if he takes the reins at Old Trafford is that he is not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools. At the World Cup, he appeared to criticise the intervention of FIFA - and President Trump – in suspending Folarin Balogun’s ban to make the striker available for a knockout clash with Belgium.

‘I feel disappointed with too many people. They put politics and manipulation, talk about ethics and integrity [first]. If we talk about the history of this game, I am disappointed in a personal way.’

With Pochettino, you’re either all in or you’re out. Look back to his time at Tottenham for evidence of that: the decision to exile stars such as Younes Kaboul, Etienne Capoue and Paulinho into a ‘bomb squad’ - and give chances to stars such as Harry Kane - was the start of his success there.

He’s a builder of teams, works with the tools he has and makes players better. Again, that sounds like the sort of thing United are crying out for.

Pochettino is big on culture – he adopted the mantra ‘culture eats strategy for breakfast’ after a meeting with the chairman of U.S. fast food chain Chick-fil-A – and worked hard to change the holiday camp feel at the USA team. Senior stars believed they did not need to put in the extra work to keep their places. The most notable example saw national team poster-boy Christian Pulisic, once of Chelsea, attempt to skip key games after a long season for AC Milan. Pochettino put a stop to that.

The Argentine does not suffer fools, is big on culture, and can deal with big club executives - his time at Tottenham taught us that

He can manage upwards, too. He handled chairman Daniel Levy well, and credited open dialogue as being key to the partnership with the chairman which yielded a runners-up finish in the Premier League and a run to the Champions League final.

‘I speak to him a lot, we talk a lot, we have very good communication,’ Pochettino said in 2018.

‘That means sometimes we agree and sometimes we don't agree. But after, when the decision is made, we are so strong in the delivery of it which shows it is best for the club’.

His cordial relationship with Levy meant Spurs were unconcerned when he met Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016 at Scott’s in Mayfair towards the end of Louis van Gaal’s troubled reign at Old Trafford.

There was nothing untoward in that - after the restaurant meeting Pochettino returned to Spurs training, and United appointed Jose Mourinho that summer.

But he was again touted as a contender when Mourinho was dismissed two years later.

Levy sacked him in 2019, but Pochettino has remained respectful and has since praised Levy’s impact.

On the field, his time at Spurs became famous for relentless intensity - a high energy approach with a high press. Think flying full-backs Danny Rose and Kyle Walker, and all-action midfielder Mousa Dembele. For another example of him getting the best from players look at Cole Palmer. The Englishman has never since replicated his numbers from 2023-24, Pochettino’s only season at Stamford Bridge.

The football, admittedly, was a little chaotic at Chelsea. It lacked control, and not even a mountain of meat could prevent him from being quizzed about his style of play in press conferences.

Chelsea’s fans never took to Pochettino. He was the face of Spurs, after all. Pochettino might be walking his dog – a Rhodesian Ridgeback called Sansa, named after the Game of Thrones character Sansa Stark – and the odd supporter would happily stop him to have a cosy chat. But he was always going to struggle to win over the supporters in their entirety.

He once said the first time he felt a connection with Chelsea’s supporters was in April 2024 after defeating Erik Ten Hag’s United 4-3, when Cole Palmer scored twice in the 10th and 11th minutes of stoppage time. That was 11 months after he joined.

He never quite won over the fanbase of Chelsea, where his football was chaotic and his high-intensity values led to accusations that he had worsened their injury crisis

One source at the time said Pochettino wanted ‘machines’ who had the physicality to play the high-energy philosophy he craved, and like at Spurs there was indeed a great deal of high-intensity running involved in training.

However, this talk of his sessions being fitness-focused led to accusations that his methods were contributing to their crippling injury list. Pochettino disputed that, telling us he did not come ‘from Mars’ and that he knew how to manage footballers better than those on social media. He was extremely defensive whenever asked if his training was primitive.

It would be fair to debate whether United have the players to play this way – and indeed how Pochettino himself would respond to the changing landscape of the Premier League.

Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi noted recently that upon his return to the Premier League after two years away that almost all clubs now play a more physical game than when he was at Brighton. With more teams doing the same thing that once made a Pochettino side different, how would he adapt?

We are told leaving his job in charge of the USA is more contractually feasible now than it was before the 2026 World Cup when Spurs made checks last season. He has a buyout clause, apparently worth around £7million, though that does not include the compensation required to recruit Perez and Co.

Should United require any character references, they need only ask their own Luke Shaw. He wrote the epilogue of Guillem Balague’s book Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs, having played under him at Southampton. Shaw admitted in those pages that he would love to work with his old coach again someday. Pochettino was there for him when Shaw broke his leg – still a man-manager even when they were no longer working together.

But United could also ask any number of Chelsea players who worked with Pochettino. They largely loved him. At the time of his dismissal in May 2024, one agent of a senior figure in the changing room told us that their client was ‘devastated’. Nicolas Jackson, formerly of Chelsea and now of Aston Villa, responded to Pochettino leaving by posting two face-palm emojis on Instagram.

Pochettino had his favourites. Conor Gallagher was one of them, and the Cobham graduate's contractual situation seemed to be a source of angst between the coach and Chelsea’s hierarchy.

Players tend to love Pochettino - Luke Shaw (right), one of Manchester United's veterans, had a strong relationship with him at Southampton

His power waned at Chelsea - the club hired a set-piece coach after he insisted he didn't want one, and he was gone before the specialist arrived

As noted, Pochettino was a builder hired to work with one of the Premier League’s youngest squads but did not get the time he wanted to mould Chelsea and never hid his desire for more power at Stamford Bridge. It is said they once had the chance to sign Ansu Fati from Barcelona on favourable financial terms, but did not go through with the transfer after the manager decided he was not for him.

We did get a glimpse of Pochettino’s waning power when Daily Mail Sport asked him once whether he would like a set-piece specialist adding to his staff. He dismissed the idea, suggesting he did not need one. Chelsea then lost the Carabao Cup final when Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk headed in the winner in extra time from a corner, with Gary Neville coining the ‘blue billion-pound bottlejobs’ jibe.

A month later, Chelsea agreed a deal to hire Bernardo Cueva from Brentford to lead a new department dedicated to set-pieces. Pochettino responded by reminding us: ‘I am the head coach and I am going to decide if some people are going to be with me or not, or if I’m going to add more people or not to the touchline.’ He was gone before Cueva arrived in the summer.

An end-of-season review was held in May 2024, and Pochettino, along with Chelsea’s hierarchy, decided after a single season that it was not working. Not for him, and not for them.

Now those at the helm of United need to determine whether he is the man to bring the good vibes back, perhaps also with a little meat.

#1728. Saliba returns with scope for rotation against Slavia Prague

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, away to Slavia Prague. There was a big boost ahead of the game with the return of William Saliba to full training, and the Frenchman is with the squad for the game this evening. Whether he starts or not is another question, but he’s clearly in good enough shape to be in contention for some minutes, and that can only be a good thing.

It was obviously a topic of conversation at the manager’s pre-game press conference yesterday evening, and provided an update on how the recovery has gone:

He’s in a really good place. I think the process and the timings and in the manner the injury has been dealt with, and especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, they’ve been very, very positive. So, his evolution has been as expected, which is not always the case. He feels very comfortable. He played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week and he feels ready to go. So whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.

There have rightfully been plenty of plaudits for Ezri Konsa since his arrival, and the way he’s slotted into the team, and there was a question about how he solves the two into three ‘problem’ when choosing his central defenders going forward:

So far we haven’t had that luxury, I wouldn’t call it a problem! We can talk about problems that are very different to that one. The moment that they are fit and available, we’re going to have the opportunity to give players rest or to load the players and to manage the congestion of the players in a much better way than we’ve actually done.

That is most definitely the kind of problem any manager would like to have. There’s no need to rush Saliba back, we can be cautious with his reintegration, and then when we have the problem of deciding who plays in which game, it feels very much like the kind of bridge we can cross when we come to it. But it’s a very nice bridge.

Beyond that, I think there’s some real room for rotation this evening. Players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will be looking for minutes at the back, and if we don’t see either Declan Rice or Martin Odegaard in the starting line-up this evening, I’d be absolutely fine with that. The manager can choose two World Cup winners in midfield, and still leave out one of Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes if he does that – it’s the kind of ‘luxury’ he needs to lean into.

Speaking about Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, he said of their involvement so far this season:

They are playing a pivotal role. If we focus on the players that are starting, obviously that’s something else. Mikel has started some games already, some important games and he’s coming from a World Cup, a very successful World Cup. We know the value of the players that we have in the squad. They need to feel important. I do think that they feel very important and we have to make sure that they continue like that because if they have that spirit and that belief within themselves every time they play, they will make things happen for the team to win the game.

Up front, it’s a little trickier. Eberechi was a doubt for the game against Liverpool, while Christos Tzolis player almost the full 90 after his return from injury. I wonder is there any scope to start Max Dowman on the right, which means you can time-share the left between the two I just mentioned and/or Noni Madueke. I think you also have to look at this as another chance for Viktor Gyokeres who did get on the scoresheet against Fleetwood, but on a night when any kind of confidence boost that might have provided was offset by the fact we lost to lower league opposition. His minutes have been a bit scarce so far this season, but you’d be very hard pressed to argue that when he has played he’s done enough to give the manager much to think about. He could really use goals and a decent performance this evening.

I suppose that defeat to Fleetwood might give Arteta some pause for thought when it comes to how much he might rotate, but if you can’t give players minutes in games like this, then they’re not going to be in the kind of shape you need them be in if and when they’re required for more challenging fixtures. It’s not to take anything for granted against a side who are top of their domestic league, but in Europe this season they’ve been a bit poor, and if this isn’t the time to test our squad depth, I don’t know what is. Let’s see!

#1727. Arsenal transfer news: Gunners in Antonio Nusa 'boost' as RB Leipzig position becomes clear

By Darren Plant | 13 Nov 2026 17:32

Arsenal have reportedly received a boost in their quest to sign RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa.

The Gunners are currently enjoying a break from action after opening up a five-point lead at the top of the Premier League table.

Nusa's six goals and eight assists from 15 appearances across all competitions has further enhanced his reputation as one of the best wingers in Europe.

Despite his status at RB Leipzig, Hinze says that the Bundesliga giants could be forced into the sale of the 21-year-old next summer.

Even if RB Leipzig earn Champions League football for 2027-28, it is claimed that they will need to generate more than €100m (£83.51m) in gross income.

Although there are other players in the first-team squad that could attract big-money proposals, Nusa's valuation is on an upward trajectory.

Furthermore, he will only have two years left on his contract from the summer onwards.

With Nusa nearly at the halfway point of his five-year deal with RB Leipzig, it feels only a matter of time before he moves elsewhere.

While there is no release clause in his contract, RB Leipzig will have a figure in mind for next summer.

Nusa has contributed a total of 16 goals and 19 assists from his 86 appearances, with 40% of those coming this season.

Arsenal will recognise the potential in Nusa at a time when it is clear that they could benefit from making an investment in a high-profile winger of Nusa's age.

His ability to play on both flanks will only encourage Arteta to give the green light to a move.

#1726. Tactics Column: High alert at the back stick

A long overdue win at Anfield was marked by a goal, a number of other Arsenal chances, and what will go down as a famous clean sheet, all involving how the two teams defend at the back post.

There were plenty of other interesting things to note on Sunday – Martin Odegaard’s role drifting across the pitch early on and Arsenal’s 20-odd minute spell of dominance midway through the second half both caught the eye – but in the latest instalment of our video series Between The Lines, I look into how Arsenal had great joy attacking the back post, and why Liverpool were never going to have the same luck at the other end.

With the hosts’ defence getting narrow in their own box, Arsenal created plenty of opportunities by having the man on the far side outside that defensive block. That’s how Kai Havertz scored, it’s how he nearly tapped in from Bruno Guimaraes’ effort that flew just wide, and it’s how Noni Madueke nearly teed Havertz up with another tap-in. It’s also where Christos Tzolis was positioned as he came onto a Madueke cross and forced Alisson into the game’s standout save.

Arsenal, though, have no such weakness: their combination of organisation, hunger, and (perhaps most importantly) focus meant Liverpool were never likely to find a spare man at the back post.

#1725. Cardinale discusses MSE creation and evolution within Milan: “Helping write a new chapter”

With the news of the new company leading AC Milan, Gerry Cardinale has offered a few words about what it means for the project.

In recent minutes, RedBird have announced a new parent company for Milan, aptly named ‘Milan Sports & Entertainment’. It’s a project that aims to put all of the club’s investments under one umbrella, whilst also allowing further investment into the city.

The new stadium is believed to have played a big part in this decision, and the Rossoneri will hopefully benefit significantly from this move.

As MilanNews relays, Cardinale offered some words in the announcement about the creation of the company, what it means to the city and for Rossoneri fans, what it means for the club.

“Over the past 25 years, we have worked alongside rights holders in the sports and media sectors to create innovative businesses that have transformed their respective industries.

“This evolution is based on a deep respect for the intellectual property assets that underpin these businesses, a long-term partnership with rights holders, and the ambition to fully unlock the potential of these teams and leagues, both on and off the pitch.

“Milan Sports & Entertainment represents the culmination of this journey and the work we have carried out since we first invested in AC Milan four years ago. Becoming a club owner has given us an even deeper understanding of what creates long-term value: winning, serving fans, and investing in the communities that give these institutions meaning.

“Today, we apply this experience on a different scale: not just to a single club, a single sport, or a single facility, but to an entire city and a portfolio that spans sports, lifestyle, and entertainment. I have known Brett Yormark and worked with him for 25 years.

“We’ve been working with Milan for years, and I can’t imagine a better executive in the international sports industry to help execute this strategy. Thanks to Brett, we can bring the best of American sports and live entertainment to Milan, helping write a new chapter in the city’s growth and international success.

“With AC Milan as our cornerstone, which will always be the driving force behind all our initiatives, we intend to build a world-class sports and entertainment platform capable of shaping the future of Milan and European sports, and bringing it back to the forefront of the global stage.”

Considering how much attention Cardinale has paid to the future of the Diavolo, and taking them back to the top level, it’s nice to hear it referenced once again in his latest statement. Hopefully this move is another step towards that.

#1723. Sebastian Pocognoli targets Tottenham star for Scotland allegiance switch from England

By Ben Sully | 13 Nov 2026 17:36, Last updated: 13 Nov 2026 17:38

Scotland Sebastien Pocognoli has admitted Tottenham Hotspur star Archie Gray is one of two Premier League players he is targeting for a potential allegiance switch from England.

Gray is currently with the England Under-21 squad after working his way through the national team age groups.

Barring any injury issues, the 20-year-old is likely to be part of Lee Carsley's squad for the Under-21 European Championships next summer.

However, progression to the England senior side is far from a foregone conclusion, partly because he is also eligible to represent Scotland.

Gray's father, Andy, represented Scotland at senior level, as did his grandfather, Frank, and his great-uncle, Eddie.

Pocognoli has admitted Gray and Everton's Hayden Hackney are his radar for potential allegiance switches to Scotland, who have not been put off by failing to convince Harvey Barnes to represent the Tartan Army under Steve Clarke.

“With Barnes it was different," Pocognoli said. "I knew before my first camp that he was different.

"The two other lads [Gray and Hackney] are young lads. It’s a long way. But if you wait too long, it might not be the right moment. In a year’s time, we will see.

“Right now, we have players in the squad who are performing well. It will always be up to them to be the priority.

"Because we’ve built things and we’ve had time with the ones who are here right now. But we are on it. We are always proactive in all of these situations.

"What is very exciting about those two names is that they are young players. That’s interesting. We have to look and manage the situation.”

Everton's Hackney made a couple of appearances for Scotland Under-21 side before going on to feature 13 times for the England Under-21s.

The 24-year-old now has to decide whether he will commit to England or Scotland, with Pocognoli feeling that the best route to convincing players like Hackney is by giving them a project to believe in.

“The best way to convince players is to show good football, show them they can come to us, enjoy it and be successful," the Scotland boss added.

“They have to feel when they leave a top club that they arrive here into top conditions and a top environment. That’s the best publicity we can offer, to show good football.”

Scotland will return to action against North Macedonia this evening, before they conclude the UEFA Nations League league phase with a game against Switzerland on Sunday.

#1722. Slavia Prague 1-2 Arsenal: Slight concerns but another away day win

Arsenal secured another away win last night, this time in the Champions League beating Slavia Prague 2-1 thanks to goals from Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres.

Mikel Arteta rotated in some areas, with starts for Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze, but relied too on the foundational stability of Declan Rice with Ezri Konsa and Gabriel behind him. We began in lively fashion, and took an early lead.

David Raya played it long, Gyokeres held it up well and hooked the ball forward, and Madueke’s pace took him beyond the defender and into the box before finishing between the keeper’s legs. Solid play from two players who can sometimes be guilty of fluffing their lines when it comes to those key actions. This time they were spot on.

We had more chances to score. Eze showed nice skills in the box but saw his shot blocked; Gyokeres headed back across goal for Merino but he headed over; the Spaniard saw a shot from distance tipped over, and his smart near post run and a right-footed shot from a Ben White cutback forced the keeper into another decent stop; and there was a brilliant counter and pass from Rice that drifted all the way to the back post without any Arsenal player attacking it for a tap-in.

We did find a second though. Gyokeres combined well with Merino around their box, and when he was played through he opened up his body really well and produced a fine finish from close range and a tight angle to make it 2-0. I don’t think that goal at Fleetwood would have done much for his confidence, this felt much more like the kind of strike he needed to produce – for himself as much as the team.

So, we had a good lead at the break, but this was very much a game of two halves. In the first we had 60% possession, out-shot the opposition by 8 to 2, and passed at nearly 90% success rate. In the second, the tables turned. Slavia Prague took 17 shots to our 4, and our pass success fell to 77%. We were sloppy and untidy, they made a tactical change at half-time which worked well for them, and while we weren’t necessarily under the cosh, the entire dynamic of the game changed and we couldn’t get to grips with it.

We needed David Raya to make one superb save to keep them at bay, before Gabriel had to head one off the line, but in injury time they found the goal I think their second half performance (and ours) probably merited. They whipped in a wicked ball from the left, the striker applied the close range finish, and the clean sheet was gone.

Afterwards, Mikel Arteta was happy with the win, but displeased with the second half, saying:

First of all, you have to value the fact it’s very difficult to win away from home. We’ve done it against a very tough opponent, we expected that toughness. In the first half we played at a really high level in terms of intensity, tempo, quality and clarity in what we had to do, and what the game was demanding. We were very efficient – we should have scored three, four or five.

I already talked about some of the things we didn’t do, and others I’d prefer not to mention. It’s a huge lesson, and we’ll learn from the second half. It’s our third away game in quick succession, and we’re the only team to have played three away games in the Champions League and just one at home – there are a lot of factors – but I don’t like to use that, because in the first half we were at the level we wanted. I take full responsibility for the drop in the second half.

I don’t think the team played well at all in the second half, but I do wonder about how we might have done things differently. For example, I feel like Declan Rice played within himself in that second period, and let me be clear, I understand why. Personally, I think it’s a bit mad he did 90+ minutes in a game like this, even if I accept he and the manager know more about his fitness than any of us. Maybe they need him to be like a steam train, going going going all the time, but when you have options of the quality of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes on the bench, surely using them in his stead allows the best of two worlds: some rest for Rice, and fresher legs in midfield when the game is tilting in the opposition’s favour.

We have this really strong bench, but I don’t think the changes we made worked particularly well. The question, of course, is if they absolutely needed to. We had a two goal lead until late on, and we secured all three points away from home after a difficult and physically demanding game at Anfield three days previously. I just found the Jekyll and Hyde nature of of the two halves a little concerning, but only a little. Ten of our sixteen games this season have been away from home, we’ve won seven of them, so that’s a decent return, added to by this victory.

Ultimately, this is essentially a forgettable Champions League tie that we came away with three points from. Apparently it was a year to the day since we played Slavia Prague last season too, a game I had/have zero recollection of. Which might say something about me more than anything else, but these kinds of fixtures don’t live long in the memory. They’re grist for the mill in this part of the season, we had a job to do, and we got it done, and now all the focus turns to Hull on Saturday and the three points required there before the Interlull.

We can talk a bit more about this game in an Arsecast a bit later on this morning, before I head to London a bit later on this afternoon. For those who have registered to come to the launch of The 22 tomorrow at Big Red, please remember you can purchase the book via the email sent to you (check your junk folders if you don’t see it), so you can simply come and collect on the night. We can also facilitate sales via credit card etc if you don’t want to do that.

If you purchased via the Patreon pre-sale, those books are not for collection tomorrow, and will be shipped to you in due course. There is also some scope to come along on spec on the night, and we should have copies available but obviously priority goes to those who registered. We will then have a final batch of books going on general sale online on Saturday evening after the Hull game. Full details of that to follow here on site and via Arseblog on BlueSky.

Ok, I’ll leave it there for now. Pod will be out mid-morning, until then, have a good one.

#1720. Is the Gyokeres iron hot enough for Hull?

I’m here for our book launch which takes place tonight, but also for our game against Hull tomorrow. Mikel Arteta will meet the press this afternoon ahead of that one, and we’ll bring you all the stories on Arseblog News. I don’t think there’s gonna be anything mind-blowing, it looked like we came through the Slavia Prague game without any issues, so fingers crossed that’s the case.

I suppose I’m mildly curious as to whether Viktor Gyokeres’ performance on Wednesday will see him keep his place up front. He got a great goal, provided an assist for Noni Madueke, and probably should have had another assist when he headed back across goal for Mikel Merino, only for the Spaniard to head over the bar when we know he can do better from those situations.

He’s a player who seems to need confidence and rhythm, and on that basis it would make some sense to keep him in the starting line-up. After the last Interlull, when he scored in four successive games for Sweden, I made the case that giving him a start in our first game back would make some sense to try and harness some of what was a good goal scoring run. Strike while the iron is hot and all that.

I looked at a home game against Leeds as the kind of fixture that would suit him. He scored two against them at home last season, and one at Elland Road, but when the time came Mikel Arteta picked Kai Havertz up front. Speaking about the decision to start Gyokeres on Wednesday in Prague, the manager said:

It was a game we believed would be really good for him, for the demands the opponent puts in and the spaces he could use. He’s done it really well, not just for the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s really great news for him, because he really needed that performance.

The question will be does Arteta think Hull at home will be as good for him as Slavia Prague away? After a bright start to the season they haven’t won any of their last seven but they have drawn five of those. Chances are they’re going to come and sit deep, using the blueprint we’ve seen many teams deploy against Arsenal in the past. If a Gyokeres game, if we can call it that, requires the opposition to leave spaces he can use (as per Arteta’s quote above), then maybe this isn’t one of those.

However, on paper, and with all due respect to tomorrow’s opposition, if Hull at home isn’t a Gyokeres game, then it’s hard not to be a bit worried. Personally, I’d be all right to see him start this one, and if it doesn’t work then you have other options. Havertz is the obvious one, but Mikel Merino is an alternative as well with his ability to find spaces inside the opponent’s penalty area. Ideally though, it’s a bit of a building block of a game for the Swedish international. We need him to deliver goals and assists, the last few weeks have been a bit more positive in that regard, and ultimately it’s important that the manager recognises the moments in a season when he might have to choose one player over another for the overall benefit of the team.

Which is to say, I look forward very much to seeing Declan Rice starting up front against Hull tomorrow, and Arteta revealing that his tech-boffins have invented a gizmo which will allow Rice to player 180 minutes in every game. Plus injury time. I kid, obviously, but I suppose we should know by now that regardless of what we think about team selections, use of players, and everything else, this manager will never be even remotely swayed by external noise – and that’s a good thing most of the time!

We will talk a bit more about the Hull game in a quick preview podcast on Patreon a little later on. Because of the book launch, we’ll be recording before the manager meets the press, so bear that in mind.

Hopefully catch lots of you later on at Big Red – and here’s a nice piece on the photos in the book. #1719. Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea

The stirring of what might yet be a great partnership between Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, although it will need to be, given some of the chaos that endures at Chelsea.

This was a Premier League game played at a furious pace, and the two former Real Madrid team-mates in charge of the sides will not have seen much of the control all coaches seek. Xabi Alonso’s team eventually won with a goal from each of his attacking triumvirate of Rogers, Palmer and João Pedro – and at times it will have been painful for the new Chelsea manager.

That was chiefly the fault of Robert Sánchez, who was embraced afterwards by Alonso, having demonstrated just how damaging a shaky goalkeeper can be to any serious team. Álvaro Arbeloa’s Fulham had their moments – and the best ones were granted to them by Sánchez. At a club that is such a restless trader of footballers, it feels remarkable that Sánchez has endured for so long.

Alonso played down the significance of Sánchez’s errors, although he cannot seriously be considering sticking to his mantra of “relax and carry on”. That was, he said, his response to the first-half Sánchez mistake that let in Josh King’s shot for Fulham’s first goal. Sánchez could have done a lot better with Gonzalo García’s goal after the break.

Fulham have equalised against Chelsea thanks to Josh King's low strike 💥 pic.twitter.com/WCLKB7XqeE

Gonzalo Garcia has scored on his Premier League debut after Robert Sanchez spilled Castagne's shot 🤯 pic.twitter.com/BmP6eqwkuN

Chelsea have a lot of faith that Mike Penders, the 21-year-old Belgian on the bench for this game, will be their first-choice goalkeeper eventually. The situation seems rather more urgent and with Penders likely to feature against Luton Town on Thursday night in the Carabao Cup it would appear a big decision is looming for Alonso.

In terms of the Palmer-Rogers axis, this was very promising, although there was no doubting the senior figure in this. Palmer’s ball set João Pedro free in the first minute, the Brazilian lifting a well-judged nudge over Bernd Leno.

"A flying start under Xabi Alonso!" Chelsea lead against Fulham after just 31 seconds 🤯 pic.twitter.com/LrkYxOReFB

It was Palmer who was crucial to the second for Rogers, made by Maxence Lacroix on his debut. Palmer stroked in the third on 49 minutes with the easy confidence of a man in form.

A goal for Morgan Rogers on his Chelsea debut! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/hphe8y077v

"Cole Palmer back to his best!"Palmer has scored to double Chelsea's lead! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/zo6e0Vdcgq

“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

“We concede goals in the first minute, the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half and there are not worse moments to concede. But we showed character and personality and I am very proud of how my players responded. We deserved a little bit more but football is not about what you deserve, it is about what you take. If you lose against a team like Chelsea they [should] have to do a little bit more. For me, they are easy goals for them and mistakes we cannot make. We need to improve and be more ready in the first minute, that is for sure.

“We are on our way and we will keep improving. The first thing I want to see is a competitive team. We were tonight, we tried our best and tried to play our football against a team like Chelsea, which is not easy. I believe in them and I believe in young players. I think they have the energy and ambition I want and they fit in the way I play. Josh King is absolutely amazing. I am really happy with him. Gonzalo [Garcia] scored and Cesar [Palacios] did well. I think they need a bit more time but they are doing great and making an impact already.”

The final whistle is blown at Craven Cottage and Chelsea hold on to win 3-2 to give Xabi Alonso a win in his first game in charge. Alvaro Arbeloa’s first game as Fulham boss ends in defeat. An absorbing west London derby.

Garcia throws himself to the ground as Sessegnon sends in a cross but that is never going to be a penalty.

Will there be one more chance for Fulham to try and find an equaliser? Time is running out for the hosts.

Pedro has the ball in the back of the Fulham net but Quenda was offside in the build-up. A quick VAR check proves so.

Surely there is another goal in this one? It is a surprise there has not been since Garcia got a goal back for Fulham.

The latest booking of the game goes the way of Castagne, who cynically trips Colwill.

Sessegnon is played in down the left channel and flicks it past Acheampong inside the Chelsea penalty area. Sessegnon gets his shot away from a narrow angle and it is straight at Sanchez.

Palmer looks like he might have cramp in his calf and is going to be replaced by Estevao. Quenda also comes on for Chelsea, coming on for Rogers.

Fulham make an attacking alteration as Muniz replaces Robinson

That is a huge, huge chance for Fulham to equalise. Robinson is played in behind the Chelsea defence with a long ball in behind and Sanchez is in no-man’s land out of his goal. Robinson just has to lift it over Sanchez from the edge of the box but his effort goes wide. Fulham should be on level terms.

Fulham fans think they are about to be awarded a free-kick right outside the box but instead the free-kick goes the other way. It was a clear dive from Bassey, who is rightly booked for simulation.

James is the third Chelsea player into the book for cynically pulling King back. James then has the cheek to wag his finger at King, as if it was not a foul, yet it was a clear booking. James had to be careful there as some referees may not have taken too kindly to that.

Double change for Fulham as Kevin and Sessegnon are brought on.

That would have been a great goal from King. He has already scored once and is inches away from his second. He receives a pass on the turn from Robinson and drives towards the Chelsea box. He then cuts inside onto his right, beating Lacroix with ease, and nearly beats Sanchez at his near post but his shot goes inches wide.

This is a very open, end-to-end game and you would fully expect more goals in this one. I would be very surprised if this one ended 3-2. Both defences are looking leaky.

Fulham are going to make their substitution of the night as Charles comes on for his debut having signed from Southampton, replacing Bobb.

Enzo is being booed a lot by the home fans every time he touches the ball.

Chelsea are the first to turn to their bench. Enzo is coming on and is met by a lot of boos, mostly though from the home fans as the majority of the travelling Chelsea fans are applauding him. Chavarria is also on to make his Chelsea debut. Hato and Lavia head off.

There is a new rule being implemented. Hato takes far too long over a throw-in and Fulham are therefore awarded the throw-in instead.

When Palmer put Chelsea 3-1 up, the visitors looked in control of this match. Fast forward five minutes and the momentum has completely switched around. What an absorbing opening Monday night of the season!

The Fulham debutant gives them life and this game is not over. Castagne is found making a run in behind and cuts back inside onto his left inside the Chelsea penalty area. His shot is straight at Sanchez, who can only parry it straight into the path of Garcia, who heads into the ground and the ball bounces over Sanchez into the Chelsea net. Another poor piece of goalkeeping from Sanchez.

Gonzalo Garcia has scored on his Premier League debut after Robert Sanchez spilled Castagne's shot 🤯 pic.twitter.com/BmP6eqwkuN

All members of Chelsea’s starting front three have got on the scoresheet tonight and Palmer also has an assist to his name.

Chelsea come close to a fourth as Hato squares it for Rogers inside the Fulham box but Robinson nips in just in front to clear.

He came close to scoring moments ago and now he does get on the scoresheet. Pedro gets onto the end of a flicked-on header by Rogers near halfway and drives into the Fulham half. As he gets to the Fulham penalty area, he waits for the overlapping run of Palmer and times the pass just right. Palmer, from a narrow angle, puts it between Leno’s legs and into the far corner.

"Cole Palmer back to his best!"Palmer has scored to double Chelsea's lead! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/zo6e0Vdcgq

Palmer does brilliantly down Chelsea’s right to skip past a number of defenders and moves into the Fulham penalty area. He opens up his body and curls one towards the far corner. He is adamant that there is a deflection but a goal kick is given. Replays show Palmer may have had a point.

Nottingham Forest are ramping up their pursuit of Chelsea’s Liam Delap as Oliver Glasner eyes two major signings before the window closes.

Forest are in talks with Chelsea over a potential loan deal for the forward after he was made available at Stamford Bridge and not included in their opening-day squad against Fulham.

Negotiations are ongoing, but Delap fits the profile of striker Forest are prioritising and is a long-term target for both the club and Glasner from his spell at Crystal Palace.

Possession: Fulham 60%-40% ChelseaShots: 7-13Shots on target: 2-5Corners: 4-3Touches in opposition box: 16-18

An absorbing first half at Craven Cottage is brought to a close and Chelsea take a 2-1 lead into the break. Pedro put them ahead inside the first minute before King equalised for Fulham. However Rogers, on his Chelsea debut, put the visitors back in front not long before half-time.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Palmer, who has run the show for Chelsea in this first half, is inches away from putting the visitors 3-1 up. Both sides have been guilty of giving the ball away in dangerous areas and Fulham do so on this occasion. Palmer then curls an effort from the edge of the box but his shot goes just wide of the far post.

The British record transfer puts Chelsea back in front on his official debut. It stems from great play from centre-back Lacroix, who finds himself in an advanced position and receives a pass from Palmer on the right side of the box. Lacroix cuts it across to Rogers, who makes no mistake from 12 yards out. Assist and goal both coming from new signings.

A goal for Morgan Rogers on his Chelsea debut! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/hphe8y077v

Fulham fail to clear a cross from James into their box and Hato’s header falls at the feet of Lavia, whose shot from close range is saved by Leno.

Is Colwill lucky to still be on the pitch? The ball is played in behind the Chelsea defence and Colwill appeared to throw his arm across King but no foul is given. That could so easily have been given as a free-kick and a second yellow card.

Rogers drives towards the Fulham box and cuts inside onto his right foot. His effort is blocked by Cuenca before James’ first-time shot is straight at Leno.

Chelsea are inches from going back in front. It stems from great work from Palmer, who drives down Chelsea’s right. His cross from the right side of the box picks out Pedro near the penalty spot. The Brazilian volleys it first time but his effort goes just wide.

Fulham are on top at the moment and Chelsea are lucky shaky as they are under the cosh inside their own box. King is playing really well, finding pockets of space down Fulham’s right and looking a real threat.

Fulham are back on level terms but it is really poor goalkeeping from Sanchez. King, who had just threatened down Fulham’s right, receives a pass from Castagne on the right touchline and takes a touch into the Chelsea box. King then fires his shot away at the near post and gets plenty of power on it but there is no way Sanchez should be beaten. He is beaten and Fulham equalise. Good strike from King but terrible keeping from Sanchez.

Fulham have equalised against Chelsea thanks to Josh King's low strike 💥 pic.twitter.com/WCLKB7XqeE

Chelsea haven’t spent all that money on Rogers for his defending, but Alonso won’t have liked the way he let Josh King to run past him to collect the ball and smash Fulham level. Rogers switched off there.

King does brilliantly to drive down Fulham’s right and flashes a dangerous ball across the six-yard box but none of his teammates are on hand to meet the cross.

Fulham are flirting with danger in and around their box and are a touch fortunate not to concede a second goal.

Down the other end, King is urged to shoot from outside the box and he obliges. It looks like it should be a fairly routine save for Sanchez but the Chelsea keeper looks uncomfortable and pushes it behind for a corner. The delivery comes to the near post and King, who lays it off the edge of the box. It comes to Palacios, who cannot guide his effort on target.

Chelsea started this game well but have lost control and are asking for trouble. The latest example sees Sanchez take too long to clear and he accidentally allows the ball to go out before clearing to gift Fulham a corner. Bobb’s delivery is headed away at the near post by James.

That is strong one-vs-one defending from Bassey. Palmer lifts the ball over the top to pick out the run of Pedro, who is dispossessed inside the Fulham box by Bassey.

Moments later, Lavia flies into a reckless challenge on Bassey and is booked. Lavia looks stunned at that decision but he is perhaps on the fortunate side that VAR did not advise the referee to have a further look at that on the screen. Lavia was out of control and could have easily been in more trouble. Two Chelsea players already into the book and were a little bit lucky.

Palmer had just one Premier League assist to his name throughout last season and has already matched that tally tonight on the opening weekend.

Colwill is in trouble. Could Chelsea go down to 10 men early? He loses possession poorly inside his own half and then resorts to hacking Bobb down with a nasty challenge. Was Colwill the last man and could Bobb have gone racing in on goal? Colwill is booked and is perhaps a touch fortunate, although what saved him is that you perhaps could not definitively say that it was a denial of a goal-scoring opportunity.

How do Alvaro Arbeloa and his Fulham side react now they are a goal down early?

With their first attack of the Xabi Alonso era, Chelsea hit the front inside the opening minute of this west London derby. Lacroix’s header from halfway finds Palmer, who plays it into the path of Pedro. The Brazilian, fresh from signing a new deal at the club, takes it in his stride and, from inside the Fulham penalty area, lifts it over Leno and into the far corner. A fine finish from Pedro and Alonso has the perfect start.

"A flying start under Xabi Alonso!" Chelsea lead against Fulham after just 31 seconds 🤯 pic.twitter.com/LrkYxOReFB

Could Joao Pedro be the man to finally lift the curse of the number nine shirt at Chelsea? Liam Delap tried and failed last season. Pedro has taken it this term and has started like a train with that early goal. Pedro has also been prolific in pre-season and has been widely tipped to be one of the Premier League’s top scorers.

Before we get going, we take a moment to remember the great Kevin Keegan, who managed Fulham in the late 1990s.

We are under way at Craven Cottage in the final game on this opening weekend of the new Premier League season.

Alvaro Arbeloa is out on the pitch for the first time in the Premier League. A friendly if not rapturous welcome from the home fans. He’s rolled his sleeves up and he’s ready to go - literally, his skinny fit jacket has sleeves rolled up tight. It looks quite uncomfortable.

It might be a new season and a new manager, but Chelsea are still doing their pre-match huddle. Fortunately, it was nowhere near the referee or the centre circle. It seemed to be captain Reece James doing all the talking.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel at Craven Cottage and we are moments away from kick-off in this west London derby. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up tonight:

Fulham: Leno; Castagne, Cuenca, Bassey, Robinson, King, Berge, Iwobi; Bobb, Garcia, Palacios.Substitutes: Lecomte, De Gougerolles, Tete, Reed, Charles, Sessegnon, Kevin, Smith Rowe, Muniz.

Chelsea: Sanchez; Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill; Gusto, Lavia, James, Hato; Palmer, Pedro, Rogers.Substitutes: Penders, Chavarria, Barco, Enzo, Neto, Gittens, Estevao, Welbeck, Quenda.

The boos for Fernandez from the Fulham fans got a lot louder when the players stepped on the pitch. Some people chanted something rather nasty beginning with ‘w’ as well.

There were a few boos from the Fulham fans when Enzo Fernandez’s name was read out ahead of kick-off. Clearly the England fans at Craven Cottage haven’t forgotten what happened against Argentina. Fernandez was booed by some Chelsea supporters in pre-season, but there were no loud jeers from the away end during the team announcements.

“During the week they had a few setbacks. With Moises [Caicedo], and with any [player], we do not want to take too much risk. They were not ready to play tonight. We need to go week-by-week but for tonight they were not ready.”

Chelsea certainly have an army of staff. I just counted 13 staff members helping the players through their warm-up. One of them is the new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee, who is carrying around a clipboard, presumably with all his set-piece tricks on it. Culture guru Willi Isa is also out there, as is former interim manager Calum McFarlane.

Chelsea’s £117m man Morgan Rogers has just run out for his warm up ahead of his competitive debut for the club. He’s kept in close contact with his best mate Cole Palmer, going through a few passing drills and doing a few keepy-ups. He looks relaxed so far.

"You NEED goals if you want to win games" ⚽️New Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa speaks about the losses of Harry Wilson and Raul Jimenez and the addition of Gonzalo Garcia 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/tbBujmljxm

The most interesting piece of Chelsea team news is that there is no Enzo Fernandez in the starting line-up, despite the surprise absence of Moises Caicedo. Instead, Romeo Lavia will partner Reece James in the centre of midfield, with Caicedo presumably injured. There is still an expectation that Manchester City will bid for Fernandez before the transfer window shuts, but the Argentine is on the substitutes’ bench. As expected, there is no place in the Chelsea squad for Nico Jackson and Liam Delap, both of whom have not travelled and are expected to leave Stamford Bridge. No more excuses. No more jam tomorrow. It is time for Chelsea to fight for the Premier League title this season. Anything else should be deemed a disappointment.

This is Chelsea version 3.0 under BlueCo, who bought the club four years ago. First there was Todd Boehly’s trolley dash, then came Behdad Eghbali’s youth club. This summer the focus has been on being Premier League-ready.

Off the pitch, the timing might be right for Boehly to be discussing the sale of his shares to Eghbali’s Clearlake Capital. But on it, Chelsea look better equipped to re-enter the title conversation than at any point in the BlueCo era.

Monday Night Fulham. ⚪️ pic.twitter.com/Oxuni9yiez

Two former Liverpool, Real Madrid and Spain teammates go head-to-head in the dugouts at Craven Cottage as Fulham host Chelsea in a west London derby to round out the opening weekend of the new Premier League season. Alvaro Arbeloa and Xabi Alonso were teammates at Liverpool, Real Madrid and Spain and both had stints as Real Madrid manager last season but have new homes in London. Arbeloa has replaced Marco Silva, who is now at Benfica, whilst Alonso is Liam Rosenior’s permanent replacement. This is the first time a manager’s Premier League debut has come against someone he also played alongside in the competition.

“I know Alonso well because I have watched so many games of his teams,” Arbeloa said. “We have to be ready, and if we want to beat them we will have to play very well. I spoke to Xabi a few days ago. But not about football; both of our families are coming to London, and we are very good friends, until Monday night [tonight]. We will be there on the touchline, so close for 90 minutes, and we will give everything for our clubs. For those 90 minutes, we are not friends.”

Arbeloa has gone back to his former club to add a couple of players in the shape of Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios. The opening weekend has not served Fulham well of late; they have won just one of their last six Premier League opening weekend fixtures. They concluded their pre-season with a 1-0 win over Stuttgart.

Chelsea have been very active in the transfer market this summer, breaking the British transfer record to sign Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa as well as adding experience through the likes of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, whilst the likes of Marc Cucurella, Andrey Santos and Trevoh Chalobah have moved on. They finished off their pre-season with a 3-1 victory over Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge just over a week ago.

“We feel ready,” Alonso said. “We have prepared the whole pre-season with some players from the first day, other ones coming later, but the desire, the ambition, the hunger to start the Premier League is already in the building each training [session] and we are looking forward to it.”

Enzo Fernandez has been strongly linked with a move away this summer, with Manchester City’s interest well-known.

“Enzo is a Chelsea player,” Alonso added. “He is a top, top player. He is training really well since he started 10 days ago with the team, very integrated. We are happy with him and he is getting ready for Monday. He is training really well, good attitude and that is what we want. He is trying his best to prepare for the kick-off of the Premier League.”

These sides finished on the same number of points (52) last season, with Chelsea finishing ahead on goal difference. It was one win apiece for each club in the two Premier League meetings last season. Nearly a year ago, Chelsea won 2-0 at Stamford Bridge whilst Fulham won 2-1 in this fixture at Craven Cottage back in January. Chelsea have won six of the past eight Premier League meetings at Craven Cottage.

#1718. Real Madrid's Endrick faces Donyell Malen dilemma over Roma loan

By Naim Beneddra | 13 Nov 2026 17:58

Real Madrid forward Endrick could find an attractive route back to regular football at Roma in January, but the remarkable form of former Aston Villa attacker Donyell Malen raises questions over the Brazilian's potential role under Gian Piero Gasperini.

The 20-year-old has struggled for opportunities since returning from his successful loan spell at Lyon, managing just 141 minutes across seven appearances for Real Madrid this season.

Roma remain interested in signing him on loan when the transfer window reopens, having already attempted to secure his services during the summer before Jose Mourinho blocked the move.

However, a potential switch to the Italian capital presents an intriguing sporting dilemma. Malen has established himself as one of Serie A's most productive forwards, scoring eight goals in his first 10 league appearances of the 2026-27 campaign.

For Endrick, whose main priority is securing consistent playing time, joining a team with such an established attacking figure could carry a familiar risk.

Malen has been outstanding since joining Roma from Aston Villa in January 2026, scoring 14 goals in 18 Serie A appearances during the second half of last season.

The Netherlands international has maintained that impressive form under Gasperini, adding eight league goals and four Champions League strikes this term.

His performances have made him a central figure in Roma's attacking system, with the Italian side emerging as genuine contenders near the top of Serie A after finishing third last season.

The competition for Endrick would therefore be considerable, particularly if he arrived expecting to operate as the team's first-choice centre-forward.

Yet an analysis published by Brazilian outlet Trivela suggests that Gasperini's tactical approach could offer the Real Madrid youngster opportunities beyond the traditional number nine position.

Roma generally operate with three central defenders, attacking wing-backs and two supporting forwards behind a central striker.

Their emphasis on aggressive pressing, direct attacking movements and exploiting spaces behind opposition defences could suit Endrick's explosive acceleration and ability to finish quickly.

Rather than competing exclusively with Malen, the Brazilian could potentially operate alongside him as a second striker, receiving possession between the lines before driving towards goal.

Malen's movement across the forward line would also provide opportunities for Endrick to attack spaces created by the Dutchman's positioning.

Such an arrangement would require tactical adjustments from Gasperini, however, and there has been no indication that the Roma manager has guaranteed Endrick a particular role.

The Italian club also possess other attacking options, including Paulo Dybala, Matias Soule and Rodrigo Mora, meaning the youngster would still face competition even if deployed behind Malen.

Interestingly, the two forwards were both on the scoresheet when Real Madrid secured a dramatic 4-3 Champions League victory over Roma on October 14.

Malen struck twice for the hosts, while Endrick came off the bench to score Madrid's equaliser before Antonio Rudiger completed the comeback.

Endrick's situation at Real Madrid has become increasingly difficult despite his encouraging performances during last season's loan at Lyon.

The former Palmeiras youngster scored eight goals in 21 appearances in France, demonstrating how regular involvement could accelerate his development.

His limited opportunities under Mourinho have since prompted renewed speculation about another temporary departure.

Speaking while on international duty with Brazil earlier this week, Endrick acknowledged that his immediate priority was simply to play more regularly.

"I just want to play. I want to be happy, to help my teammates... to score goals and provide assists, just as I did at Lyon, which was one of the best things that's ever happened to me and one of the happiest times of my life," he told reporters.

"I don't know what will happen in January. That's in God's hands. I'm only 20 and I'll see what happens. I just ask to do what's best for my career."

Roma's interest remains genuine, with La Repubblica reporting this week that the club are monitoring the Brazilian's situation as they consider January attacking reinforcements.

However, Sporting Lisbon have also emerged as serious contenders for Endrick's signature, with former Lyon manager Paulo Fonseca reportedly keen on a reunion.

That connection could prove significant, given the improvement Endrick showed during their previous spell together in France.

Meanwhile, Mourinho's previous decision to reject Roma's approach remains another obstacle, with Real Madrid yet to approve a January departure.

Roma can offer Champions League football, a competitive Serie A environment and a tactical system that appears suited to Endrick's attacking qualities.

Whether those advantages outweigh the prospect of competing with Malen for minutes could be crucial if the Italian club succeed in reopening negotiations.

For a player who has started just once for Real Madrid this season, the possibility of playing alongside Roma's leading scorer may be appealing, but any January decision will also depend on how regularly Gasperini can accommodate him.

#1717. Are you ok, Noni?

Arsenal’s squad construction has given them a lot of depth and diversity in terms of profiles. Timber and White for right-back, Calafiori and Hincapie for left-back. Ezri Konsa has, incredibly, offered both protection and threat to the impregnable Saliba and Gabriel partnership. Bruno and Lewis Skelly, Rice and Zubimendi and Odegaard and Merino for midfield.

Eze and Tzolis for the left-wing. Havertz and Gyokeres for centre-forward. Of course, some of these pairings are more symbiotic than others. Mosquera is probably going to fall behind Konsa as a back up to either one of Saliba or Gabriel. In reality, Zubimendi is only going to play ahead of Rice if Rice is injured or Arsenal have a nice easy game against League Two opposition, for example…

On the face of it, Noni Madueke should really be in that third layer of the squad with Mosquera, Kepa and where Zubimendi probably now resides. The role of back-up to Bukayo Saka ought to have been one with limited opportunity. In a sense, I was always a little surprised that Madueke signed up for it when he came to the club from Chelsea last summer.

I was slightly surprised that Arsenal spent so much money on a player who was always incredibly unlikely to dislodge Saka no matter how much he improved. And how much scope was there going to be for Madueke to get the sort of rhythm and consistency of selection to hone his talents?

Now I strongly suspect that Arsenal would have had anxieties over Saka’s ability to stay fit after tearing his hamstring in December 2024 and missing a few months of football. It was the first significant injury Saka had incurred and after quickly deciding that loanee winger Raheem Sterling was not going to be an adequate replacement, they amended for his absence with a blend of 17-year-old Ethan Nwaneri and surplus left-back Kieran Tierney.

It isn’t difficult to see how Arsenal viewed the right-wing spot as a single point of failure but encouraging Madueke to see it as an attractive position must have challenged even Mikel Arteta’s powers of persuasion. Yet just over a year on from signing for Arsenal, Madueke has a league title winners medal (‘while others are tweeting and posting’) with 25 starts to his name last season, 16 of which were in the Premier League.

In reality, being Bukayo Saka’s third leg has, to this point, proved to be a savvy career move for Madueke because he is getting plenty of time on the pitch in Saka’s increasing absences. This extends to the England National Team too, where Madueke plays the same role. But it was a role that still earned him four starts for his country in a World Cup, including a start in the quarter-final against Norway.

A Premier League title winners medal, a Champions League Final appearance and four World Cup starts was not a bad return for Madueke in terms of playing time. I think we knew when Arsenal bought him that Noni was a talented but phlegmatic player, relentless in taking on his full-back but the quality of his end-product could vary markedly.

In his new signing profile of Madueke on Arseblog, Phil Costa wrote, ‘there’s a feeling that Arsenal lack penetration from their wingers (Bukayo Saka aside); chaos factor, some unpredictability, and Madueke brings this in spades. His first thought when receiving the ball is centred around provoking defenders and driving towards goal, which means you can isolate him without too much focus on the overall setup – you just wind him up and let him go.

‘There are two specific metrics to love when assessing the 23-year-old; per FBRef data, he currently sits in the 95th percentile for progressive carries (6.82 per 90) and the 98th percentile for carries into the box (4.12 per 90). Those are big numbers.’ There was never any doubt about Madueke’s ability to get the ball into threatening areas, the question has always been what he does when he gets there.

Last season, some clips of him harumphing the ball out of the stadium on his right foot went semi-viral. I also think some of his performances were impacted by a lack of balance in the front three. With technicians like Havertz and Odegaard unavailable, he was often playing alongside fellow blunderbusses like Gyokeres and Martinelli.

I admit that my tolerance for inefficiency is high when it comes to attackers. I think attacking is a volume game. The vast majority of attacks come to nothing, the vast majority of shots do not go in or even work a goalkeeper. Individual attacks are the weather but, overall, attacking is the climate. The more you do it and sustain it, the more likely you are to score.

So my ‘we can fix him’ gene for slightly wayward wingers is high. I didn’t even mind Gervinho (a frustrating player, no doubt, but the Bradford miss has become the defining image of his Arsenal career which I don’t believe was fully representative of his performances).

The video of Madueke’s right foot ballooning the ball into the upper tier against Kairat last season has been refined. Both his goals this season have been on his right foot, particularly notably against Nottingham Forest where he cut in on his right and unleashed a low and controlled shot. It might have taken a helpful deflection but that’s because he kept the attempt low.

Last season, his right footed efforts were more in danger of colliding with low flying aircraft on their way into orbit. Noni’s goal against Slavia Praha demonstrated his pace in behind. It was the sort of goal and chance Gabriel Martinelli was hoovering up in Europe last season. European games tend to offer more space in behind and with Martinelli gone, Madueke is one of the few Arsenal attackers explosive enough to exploit it.

Indeed, in my view, he ought to have won Arsenal a match winning penalty in Budapest against Paris Saint Germain in May. There are signs of greater maturity and efficiency in his game. According to WhoScored.com his pass success rate in the Premier League last season was 76.2%. This season so far it is 86.3%.

I think he has learned that he does not have to go for the full-back at 100mph every single time he gets the ball and has varied his game. In the Champions League game against Lille, he sent 15 crosses into the penalty area, having sent six into the area in the game before against Leeds. 15 crosses sounds like a lot but it was very clearly under instruction from Mikel Arteta.

After that Lille game, the manager said of Madueke, ‘I said when you talk about players being ‘clinical’, sometimes that means scoring five in every 100. It’s about generating volume, more actions and getting him into the good positions, because he will decide matches. He had a really big contribution a few days ago, today he had a contribution in the last final pass as well.’

Being omitted from the England squad in September, according to Arteta, provided additional motivation for Noni, ‘After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him.’

He has now been omitted from the England squad again for the November international round. It is a decision I don’t really understand from Thomas Tuchel but I am happy if it continues to provide Madueke with an additional reason to fine tune his game and because it hopefully protects a player who has become very important.

I admit I am not entirely sure how good Madueke is going to be in, say, three years’ time. He is 24 and it’s at that age that attackers typically start to increase their decisive actions. He has Max Dowman in the rearview mirror too. I think Madueke has a really high ceiling and there are small, but encouraging, signs of improvement.
